verdict.headline: Houthis widen strikes on Saudi energy sites as data shows OPEC output already down
verdict.label: WTI settled +2.43% at $93.70 for a sixth straight gain after Saudi Arabia halted operations at several energy facilities; the Dow fell 1.18% against the Nasdaq's 0.32%, the ten-year rose one basis point to 4.794% and gold fell 0.84%
verdict.rationale_short:
Two pieces of evidence landed together on Tuesday. Yemen's Houthis ran a broad offensive against Saudi Aramco sites at Abha, Najran and Jizan and an air base at Khamis Mushait, wounding 73 people and forcing Saudi Arabia's energy ministry to halt operations at several facilities; explosions were reported the same day on Iran's Kharg Island, which handles roughly 90% of Iranian crude exports. Separately, a Bloomberg survey put OPEC's August production at 19.91 million barrels a day, down 900,000, with Saudi output falling just over a million barrels to 6.98 million and Saudi exports down nearly a third to 3.03 million. October WTI settled $2.22 higher at $93.70, a sixth consecutive gain, and Brent rose 1.67% to $98.61 after trading as high as about $99.50.

What separates Tuesday from the sessions before it is that the barrels are already gone rather than merely at risk. Monday's constraint was conversion capacity — refineries damaged, the diesel crack at a record, retail diesel at $5.90 a gallon. Tuesday's target list was distribution and export infrastructure on both sides of the conflict: the Aramco terminals at Abha and Najran feed Saudi domestic supply, and Kharg Island is where the large majority of Iran's crude leaves the country. A refinery outage raises a margin; an export terminal outage removes volume.

The market's response was narrow rather than defensive, and that is the part worth weighing. The Dow fell 1.18% to 52,786.07, but the Nasdaq lost only 0.32% to 26,421.41, the S&P 500 0.58% to 7,673.52 and the Russell 2000 0.52% to 2,960.20. A 2.43% move in crude bought roughly one basis point at the long end: the two-year rose 1.7 basis points to 4.396%, the ten-year 1.0 to 4.794% and the thirty-year 0.5 to 5.251%, leaving 4.818% untested for a fourth session. The VIX closed at 15.61. Gold fell 0.84% to about $4,368 an ounce on a day of escalation, and the dollar index slipped to 98.83.

A haven selling off while rate expectations rise locates the bid in policy rather than in fear. Hike odds for the September 15-16 FOMC sit near 60% after last week's payrolls print, and the marginal seller of gold and duration appears to be pricing a Fed response to inflation rather than the inflation itself. The New York Fed's August consumer survey supports that reading from the other direction: one-year inflation expectations eased to 3.58% from 3.63% and the three-year measure to 3.2% from 3.3%, despite record retail diesel prices. That was the specific test this morning's report set for the household channel, and it came back negative.

The morning read was right on structure and one step behind on the target. It called a cost rotation rather than a retreat, and the close matched: the Dow underperformed the Nasdaq by 86 basis points, energy equities led, and the front end of the curve barely moved. It located the shortage in refining margin; the day's news put it in production and export volumes instead.

The equity split was AI capital spending against everything else. Oracle rose about 5% intraday and CoreWeave 3% on a Morgan Stanley target increase, which is what held the Nasdaq's loss to a third of the Dow's — an offset the Dow does not carry. That offset is testable on Thursday, when Oracle reports first-quarter fiscal 2027 results after the close against consensus near $19.1 billion in revenue, with options pricing a move of roughly 11%.

The evidence does not all point one way. Six straight sessions of crude gains with the ten-year still 2.4 basis points below 4.818% could equally mean the bond market has not yet repriced the supply loss rather than that it has judged it contained; the OPEC survey is August data reported after the fact, and September will be worse if the Saudi outages persist. Against that, Iran said last week a Hormuz transit agreement with Oman was in its final stages, and a signed deal would take premium out of crude without restoring a barrel of refining capacity. One reference level broke on Tuesday — the S&P 500 closed below 7,700. WTI through $95, which is 1.4% away, alongside the ten-year through 4.818% would say energy has begun setting the long end and the cost read has become a rates problem; the ten-year going through alone would point at supply and this week's Treasury buyback operations instead.
verdict.lede_short: The Houthis widened their offensive to Aramco sites at Abha, Najran and Jizan, Saudi Arabia halted operations at several energy facilities, and a survey showed OPEC output already 900,000 barrels a day lower in August. WTI settled up 2.43% for a sixth straight gain, but the ten-year rose one basis point, gold fell 0.84% and household inflation expectations eased to 3.58%. WTI at $95 and the ten-year at 4.818% are the levels that would change that.

supporting_data.label: Houthi drones and ballistic missiles hit Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jizan plus the Khamis Mushait air base, wounding 73, and Saudi Arabia halted operations at several energy sites — the first time in this conflict that the kingdom has taken plants offline itself rather than absorbing a single strike

A Bloomberg survey put OPEC's August crude output at 19.91 million barrels a day, down 900,000, with Saudi production falling just over a million to 6.98 million and Saudi exports down nearly a third to 3.03 million — the barrels are already gone, which moves this from a risk premium priced in futures to volume missing from the physical market

Brent rose 1.67% to $98.61 and traded as high as about $99.50 intraday, with October WTI settling $2.22 higher at $93.70 — a sixth consecutive advance that leaves WTI 1.4% below the $95 level tracked here

The two-year Treasury yield rose 1.7 basis points to 4.396%, the ten-year 1.0 to 4.794% and the thirty-year 0.5 to 5.251% as the Dow fell 628.18 points — a 2.43% move in crude bought roughly one basis point at the long end, and 4.818% went untested for a fourth session

Gold fell 0.84% to about $4,368 an ounce on an escalation day, with the dollar index at 98.83 and hike odds for the September 15-16 FOMC near 60% — a haven selling off while rate expectations rise locates the bid in policy, not in fear

New York Fed one-year consumer inflation expectations eased to 3.58% from 3.63% and the three-year measure to 3.2% from 3.3% — households have not repriced despite record retail diesel, which was the specific test the morning report set and it came back negative

watchlist_mentions.note: Fell 1.17% to about $319 into Wednesday's product event, the first under CEO John Ternus, with a foldable iPhone and the iPhone 18 Pro line expected. A sub-2% move on the eve of a launch is the market declining to pre-position rather than a judgement on the hardware. The stock did not act as the defensive mega-cap on a day the Dow fell 628 points.

October WTI settled $2.22 higher at $93.70, up 2.43% and a sixth consecutive gain, after the Houthi offensive on Aramco facilities and reported explosions on Iran's Kharg Island. $95 is 1.4% away and remains the regime threshold. The August OPEC survey showing Saudi output down over a million barrels a day is backward-looking; September will be worse if the halted facilities stay offline.

Traded near $78,475, down about 0.9% on the day and $475 above the $78,000 downside reference, a sixth session below $80,000. It has taken no bid from the energy escalation in either direction, which is consistent with gold falling 0.84% on the same day and points at rate expectations rather than at a haven flow.

No company news on Tuesday, but the Asian memory bid that drove Monday's Kospi rally reversed: the Kospi closed 0.6% lower at 6,954.52 and the Nikkei fell 1.7% to 65,269.33, giving back most of Monday's gains. Monday's move rested on a KB Securities estimate of memory inventories below ten days of supply, and Micron's next quarterly report is still the first company data able to test it.

trade_setups.asset: WTI at $95 against the ten-year at 4.818%
trade_setups.thesis: Crude has risen six straight sessions while the long end has barely moved. October WTI settled at $93.70, 1.4% below $95, after the Houthi offensive forced Saudi Arabia to halt operations at several energy facilities and a survey put August OPEC output 900,000 barrels a day lower. The ten-year closed at 4.794%, up one basis point, and the thirty-year at 5.251%. Either the bond market has judged the supply loss contained, or it has not yet repriced it — the two are indistinguishable at this distance from the level.
trade_setups.entry: $95 on WTI and 4.818% on the ten-year, 2.4 basis points away. Wednesday's EIA weekly report at 10:30 AM ET is the first supply data since the Saudi facilities went offline; distillate stocks were last 104.2 million barrels, roughly 14% below the five-year average.
trade_setups.invalidation: A signed Iran-Oman Hormuz transit agreement, described last week as days away, would take premium out of crude without restoring refining capacity. Crude retreating while the diesel crack holds would separate the two constraints rather than resolve either.
trade_setups.horizon: This week, into the September 15-16 FOMC

trade_setups.asset: The gap between producer and household inflation
trade_setups.thesis: The two channels are moving in opposite directions. Retail diesel set consecutive records at $5.90 a gallon and the diesel crack spread is at a record above $106 a barrel, but New York Fed one-year consumer inflation expectations eased to 3.58% from 3.63% in August and the three-year measure to 3.2% from 3.3%. August PPI prints Thursday against forecasts near 5.2% after July's 4.7%, and CPI follows on Friday, with the FOMC in blackout through September 17 so no official can frame either.
trade_setups.entry: 5.2% on Thursday's PPI is the forecast; 3.58% is where household expectations now sit. A hot PPI against a contained CPI leaves the pass-through question open into the decision.
trade_setups.invalidation: A PPI print at or below July's 4.7% despite record diesel would say the freight pass-through is slower than the refining margin implies, leaving the August payrolls report as the only hawkish input still standing.
trade_setups.horizon: Thursday and Friday, into the September 15-16 FOMC

trade_setups.asset: The AI capital-spending offset that narrowed Tuesday's index decline
trade_setups.thesis: The Nasdaq lost 0.32% against the Dow's 1.18% because Oracle rose about 5% intraday and CoreWeave 3% on a Morgan Stanley target increase — an analyst revision, not a company disclosure. That offset is what kept a 628-point Dow decline from reading as a broad de-rating, and it is unverified until Thursday, when Oracle reports first-quarter fiscal 2027 results after the close against consensus near $19.1 billion in revenue and cloud growth guided at 58% to 64%.
trade_setups.entry: Options are pricing a move of roughly 11% on the print. The Dow-to-Nasdaq spread, 86 basis points on Tuesday, is the measure of whether the offset survives it.
trade_setups.invalidation: The Nasdaq joining the Dow at similar magnitude would say the market is selling equity risk broadly rather than repricing input costs. Oracle and CoreWeave giving back the target-driven gains before the print would say the same from the other side.
